title: Marcus' blind spots
hookLine: Christians were persecuted in his reign, and he made his son Commodus heir: admiration and honesty together

lines: A HUNDRED DAYS IN HIS NOTEBOOK.
cards: We've just spent more than a hundred days inside one man's notebook. We've heard him talk himself out of anger, into kindness, toward death without fear. It's easy, after that long, to start treating him like a saint.
But Marcus Aurelius was also a Roman emperor, with an emperor's power, for nineteen years. And two facts from his reign sit uneasily beside the notebook. The path doesn't skip them.

teach.h: JUSTIN AND LYON: DEATHS IN HIS REIGN.
teach.b: First, the Christians. During Marcus's reign, Christians were put to death in several places. Around the year 165 in Rome, the teacher Justin was tried and executed.
The judge was the city prefect, Junius Rusticus, the same Rusticus whom Marcus thanks in book one for lending him the works of Epictetus.
In 177, in Lyon in Gaul, a group of Christians were tortured and killed, a story preserved by the church historian Eusebius. Historians debate how much Marcus directed any of this.
There was no single empire-wide order, and much was local. But it happened under his rule, and some cases reached him.
The Meditations mention Christians once, briefly and coldly, and even that line may have been added by a later hand.
For most of the century before Marcus, emperors had passed power to adopted heirs chosen for ability, partly because they had no surviving sons. Marcus had one, and made him co-emperor in 177.

When Marcus died in 180, Commodus ruled for twelve years, and ancient historians remember those years as cruel and chaotic. Third, what to do with this. Not to throw the notebook away, and not to explain the facts away.
The man who wrote about kinship with every human mind also governed an empire that killed people for their faith. Both are true. Fourth, why it matters for us.
Every person we admire, a teacher, a parent, a hero, comes with blind spots.
Learning from someone doesn't require pretending they had none.

how: Many modern readers of the Meditations read them alongside the history of Marcus's reign, including the persecution of Christians and the succession of Commodus.

o: Marcus's son and heir, remembered as cruel once he ruled
Marcus's adoptive father, who taught him to be gentle
a Christian teacher put to death during Marcus's reign

games.q: Marcus' blind spots. tap the pairs.
p: Christian teacher executed in Rome, c. 165
the judge, and Marcus's own teacher

s: Marcus issued a single empire-wide order to persecute Christians
historians find no such order; much was local, though it happened under his rule.
the judge at Justin's trial was Rusticus, whom Marcus thanks in book one
the same Rusticus who lent him Epictetus.
before Marcus, several emperors in a row had chosen adopted heirs
Marcus, with a surviving son, made Commodus co-emperor in 177.

games.q: you've loved a teacher's book for months. then you learn about something wrong done on their watch. what does the path suggest?
o: keep both the admiration and the honesty.
games.why: the path keeps the notebook and the history together. both are true of Marcus, and of most people we admire.

practice: Bring to mind someone you admire, living or dead, and let yourself feel what you admire in them; then, gently, let one real failing come into view too.
Notice the urge to push one of them away, and try not to: hold both at once, like two stones in your hands.

wordCard.voice: Commodus. The son Marcus made co-emperor, remembered by ancient historians as cruel and chaotic once he ruled alone. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: both at once. Admiration and honesty can share one pair of hands. See you tomorrow.
